insider_note: The integrating factor here works out to a clean x², not a trig expression — a good check that the answer is on track is that ∫(2/x)dx = 2 log x = log x² collapses to a power of x, not a fraction or a log left standing.

steps.label: Identify P and Q
steps.margin_note: One mark. The equation is already in the standard linear form dy/dx + Py = Q.
steps.memory_tip: 2 log x = log x² — a log with a coefficient always collapses to a log of a power.
lines: Given D.E is dy/dx + y(2/x) = 2x². This is a linear D.E in y.
It is in the form dy/dx + yP(x) = Q(x) where P(x) = 2/x and Q(x) = 2x²
∴ ∫P dx = ∫(2/x) dx = 2 log x = log x²
steps.why: The equation is already in the exact standard form, so P and Q can be read off directly, and integrating P = 2/x gives 2 log x, which is more useful written as log x² for the next step.
common_mistakes: Reading P as 2 instead of 2/x, missing the /x.
Leaving ∫P dx as 2 log x without converting it to log x², which makes the integrating factor harder to simplify.

steps.label: Find the integrating factor
steps.margin_note: One mark. e^(log x²) = x² — the exponential and log cancel directly.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever ∫P dx is a log, the I.F. simplifies to the plain expression inside that log.
lines: Now, I.F. = e^(∫P(x)dx) = e^(log x²) = x²
steps.why: Writing ∫P dx as log x² in the previous step means the integrating factor simplifies immediately, since e raised to a log of something returns that something.
common_mistakes: Writing the I.F. as 2 log x instead of exponentiating it to x².
Computing I.F. as x instead of x², missing the square from log x².

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: Two marks. x²·2x² = 2x⁴, which integrates by the plain power rule.
steps.memory_tip: ∫2x⁴ dx = 2x⁵/5 — the standard power rule, one power up and divide by the new power.
steps.why: Multiplying Q by the integrating factor gives a plain power of x, so the right side integrates by the ordinary power rule; multiplying the whole equation by 5 at the end clears the fraction and matches the book's marked form, with the constant relabelled.
common_mistakes: Losing the factor of 2 in front of x⁴ when setting up the integral.
Forgetting to also multiply the constant term by 5 when clearing the /5, and writing 5yx² = 2x⁵ + 5c as if 5c and c were different constants — they are not, since c is arbitrary.
